title: Lens: module boundaries and dependency direction
summary: Dependencies run in the intended direction at the core but not above it. domain/ (11 modules) imports only the standard library. 25 of the 27 contracts modules import only pydantic, contracts and domain. The two exceptions are contracts/export.py, which imports api.app (the service's one upward import), and contracts/adapters.py, which imports persistence. Above that line, application/ and adapters/ import each other (21 and 26 statements) and application/ imports operations/ 6 times. The worker imports the API entry point to get its configuration. 7 of the 29 function-level imports (in 17 functions) exist only to break five module cycles, and no check reports those cycles. application/goal_loop.py is the hub. It builds the tool registry from 11 adapter imports, wires Deep Agents, and shares private lifecycle helpers with workflow_runner and 10 test files. Because the catalog and four API routers depend on it, building the API or the OpenAPI document imports 110 autobots modules, plus deepagents, langchain and langgraph. Business rules also cross layers: the GitHub adapters run approval and receipt SQL through ToolContext's raw connection, the API routes read the workspace model policy six times and write it with their own version check, and the web re-implements the run command guards. The web boundary itself holds: no client module imports a server-only module, pages are thin, and responses are parsed with generated parsers. However, 28 request bodies and 78 API paths are hand-written, and 74 of the 78 generated operations go unused. The layout has drifted from DH-03 (no workers/ or graphs/, operations/ and persistence/ undocumented, no scripts/db/). Five rule path globs match no file, and their harness test checks paths that don't exist. Nothing enforces layer direction.

scores.why: DH-06 separation holds for domain by convention only: no lint rule or test checks import direction, and five rule globs fail DH-03's 'test representative paths'.
domain and contracts are clean leaves (two contracts files aside), but application and adapters depend on each other, goal_loop is a hub, and five cycles sit behind function-level imports.
The modules with the most cross-layer edges are also among the largest (goal_loop: 782 lines, 17 application and 11 adapter imports); the area reviews cover per-file size.
Route handlers such as post_run run whole use cases, and lifecycle functions are named private while other modules depend on them.
CODEBASE.md documents the real layout, but it differs from DH-03 in five places and the rule globs follow DH-03's paths.
The pure app factory and single BFF are sound; registry, executor and model wiring happen inside application, and configuration is read at call sites.
Every module has a docstring, and 87 of 139 cite a decision, PRD or story ID; of the 7 function-level imports that break a cycle, only goal_loop.py:433 says why, and tools.py:1 is stale.
Generated parsers check responses, but request bodies use no generated types, the pool is Any in 10 copies, and SQL rows are positional tuples.
Typed refusal codes cross layers cleanly, but HTTP mapping is spread over per-router as_api_error functions, two of them with the same name.
Parity tests pin the parallel tool tables, but 34 test imports of private names couple tests to internals, and nothing tests layering.
Most changes stay in one area. Adding a tool, changing the run lifecycle or changing a request contract touches several layers with no checks to guide the edit.

strengths.title: Pure domain layer
strengths.evidence: All 11 modules in services/agent/src/autobots/domain import only the standard library and each other (AST scan: 0 framework imports and 0 imports from other layers). domain/runs.py:22-128 holds the canonical transition table and domain/execution.py:14-49 holds the execution contract.

strengths.title: Contracts are nearly a leaf, with strict configs
strengths.evidence: 25 of 27 contract modules import only pydantic, contracts and domain. contracts/primitives.py:9-10 STRICT_CONTRACT refuses unknown fields, and request models such as RunRequest (contracts/run_commands.py:16) forbid extras.

strengths.title: One OpenRouter factory
strengths.evidence: ChatOpenRouter and openrouter.OpenRouter are constructed only in services/agent/src/autobots/adapters/models/factory.py (lines 95-110 and 124). Every other model path goes through that factory, as DH-06 requires.

strengths.title: Pure app factory, lifespan-owned resources, one API composition root
strengths.evidence: api/app.py:41-92 builds the app without opening anything and opens and closes the pool in lifespan. api/main.py:37-51 is the only place that wires the environment, membership and storage for the API process.

strengths.title: Explicit web server/client boundary
strengths.evidence: apps/web/lib/bff.ts, session.ts, server-config.ts, service-status.ts and workspace-choice.ts each start with import "server-only", and none of the 39 "use client" modules imports them. lib/ imports no component, app/ has no client module, the largest page is 127 lines (app/page.tsx), and process.env is read only in lib/server-config.ts:11-21.

strengths.title: Single BFF choke point for API traffic
strengths.evidence: Every route handler that reaches the API (5 of the 8) forwards through apps/web/lib/bff.ts forward (71-126) or streamFrom (132-175). These apply the Host/Origin/CSRF guard, session, internal token, workspace header, body limits and no-store in one place. The session, workspace and csrf handlers stay local and assemble the guard themselves (XDUP-12 in the duplication lens).

strengths.title: Responses parsed with generated parsers
strengths.evidence: 25 web files import 32 distinct generated parse* functions (45 imports), for example apps/web/components/run-controls.tsx:3-6 and the parseRunSummary call at :66-68.

strengths.title: Parallel tables pinned by tests
strengths.evidence: services/agent/tests/test_execution_contract.py:23-29 keeps domain TOOL_VERSIONS equal to the registry. test_tool_catalog.py:23-31 keeps the catalog equal to the registry, and test_tool_guides.py:25-28 keeps the guides complete. domain/execution.py:14 names its test.

findings.evidence:
goal-composer.tsx:288-298:
```
const reply = await csrfFetch("/api/v1/runs", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID() },
  body: JSON.stringify({ goal_text: draft, budget_micro_usd: budget,
    ...(sessionId === null ? {} : { session_id: sessionId }), ...
```
A grep of apps/web/components finds 28 `body: JSON.stringify(` request bodies in 18 files and 78 hand-written '/api/...' path literals in 31 files. There are 0 references to a generated request type (RunRequest, ExpertCreate, ApprovalDecision, ModelPolicyUpdate, ...) and 0 uses of `satisfies`. The generated client has 78 typed operations, for example generated.ts:9418 admitRun(options, body: RunRequest), and 4 are used, all server-side.
findings.impact: Renaming or retyping a request field in Pydantic regenerates the TypeScript types but breaks no compile. The API then rejects the body (extra='forbid') with a generic 422 invalid_request (errors.py:29-32), and the screens misreport it: the composer turns any 422 into 'That model or request isn't approved' (goal-composer.tsx:331-333 and 636) and the session panel into 'That request isn't approved' (session-panel.tsx:76-77), which points the person at their model choice rather than at a contract mismatch. Path and method changes are just as invisible to tsc. Drift at the browser-to-API boundary is caught only if a browser test covers that form.
findings.recommendation: Route browser calls through the generated operations. Use a client-safe options object with baseUrl '/api' and a fetch adapter over csrfFetch, add a runtime error type that carries the parsed ErrorResponse so screens keep their refusal messages, and teach the generator to emit declared header parameters such as Idempotency-Key. Migrate one screen at a time; until a screen moves, type its bodies with `satisfies` and the generated request type.

scripts/generate_contracts.py: emit declared header parameters (Idempotency-Key) in each operation
apps/web/lib/api.ts: browserApi: ClientOptions = { baseUrl: "/api", fetch: adapter that uses csrfFetch for writes }
components: await admitRun(browserApi, body), with body typed as RunRequest; catch ApiRefusal for the refusal text

findings.evidence: Per grep, os.environ appears in 26 modules, and 19 distinct AUTOBOTS_* variables are read in 10 modules across api, application, adapters and operations. DEFAULT_KEY_FILE and its override are defined twice (api/main.py:17-26 and application/tool_keys.py:29, 77-78). The disk readiness rule reads AUTOBOTS_MIN_FREE_BYTES and AUTOBOTS_CONFIG_ROOT separately in the API (operation_routes.py:87, 95) and in the worker (worker.py:184-185), although the worker's comment says a routine 'waits on the same readiness a person would'. The worker takes its provider context from api/main.py, so it imports every api module (all 20, plus the package), every router included. key_sources(..., os.environ) is called in 6 places.
findings.impact: No single place lists what a process needs, and defaults can diverge between API and worker. Application functions that default to `environ = os.environ` silently read the real environment in tests unless every caller passes one.
findings.recommendation: Add a leaf config module that each entry point loads, and pass the config (or the environ Mapping) down. Share one installation_conditions() between operation_routes and the worker, define the master-key default once, and move provider_context_from_environment out of api/main.py.

findings.title: Nothing enforces layer direction, and function-level imports hide five cycles

locations.note: ruff selects no tidy-imports or import-outside-top-level rule
cronjob_tool -> operations.worker -> goal_loop -> cronjob_tool
experts -> tool_catalog -> assignments -> experts (again at :65)

tool_gateway <-> tool_uses (again at :402)
the only function-level import that says why

findings.evidence: An AST scan finds 0 cycles among module-level imports, but 29 function-level import statements of autobots modules, in 17 functions across 13 files. 7 of the statements break real cycles: cronjob_tool/worker/goal_loop, experts/tool_catalog/assignments (twice), routines/tool_catalog/goal_loop/cronjob_tool, goal_loop/workflow_runner and tool_gateway/tool_uses (twice). Only goal_loop.py:433 explains its import. Package edges outside the intended direction: application -> adapters 21, application -> operations 6, adapters -> operations 2, operations -> api 1, contracts -> api 1, contracts -> persistence 1. No test or lint rule checks any of them; pyproject.toml:47 selects E, F, W, I, B, UP, ASYNC and RUF, and the exploratory ALL run counts 31 PLC0415 hits.
findings.impact: New upward imports and cycles land without notice. Reviewers have to rediscover the intended direction every time, and a function-level import reads like a performance choice when it hides a cycle.
findings.recommendation: Add a pytest that builds the layer graph with ast, function-level imports included, and checks it against an allowed matrix with today's exceptions as a shrinking baseline. It should also fail on new module cycles. Require a one-line reason on each remaining function-level import. The test needs no new dependency and runs in the fast profile.

findings.evidence:
Per grep of `from autobots.api.settings_routes`, 12 of the 14 router modules import current_workspace, require_owner or provider_settings from settings_routes.py. run_routes and workflow_routes also import operation_routes.require_ready, and workflow_routes imports run_routes.budget_error.
```
def _pool(request: Request) -> Any:
    pool = request.app.state.pool
    if pool is None:
        raise ApiError(503, "service_unavailable", "The database is unavailable.")
    return pool
```

findings.evidence: The two aliases share a name but take different arguments, and both the worker and cronjob_tool write a local closure to convert between them.

rejected.title: Tool implementations are spread over 17 modules in two layers, named four different ways
rejected.reason: Mostly taste, and subsumed by XMOD-01. The counts hold (31 ToolDefinition constructions in 17 modules), but the split follows a rule: external-provider clients sit in adapters/, database-backed and feature tools beside their feature in application/. XMOD-01's registry module becomes the single index of tools, and the proposed package move is churn with checkpoint-path risk that the finding itself defers. The stale docstring at application/tools.py:1 ('Nothing else exists' above five tools) is a single-file comment issue for the py-tools area.

notCovered: This lens covers patterns across the 545 in-scope files. I opened the code behind every cited pattern but did not read every file in full; the area reviews cover single files. Large modules I read only in part include goal_loop, workflow_runner, tool_catalog, tool_gateway, approvals, run_routes, settings_routes, operations/worker, loop_middleware, the GitHub adapters, goal-composer and run-controls. The Python import analysis is static (ast): it counts module-level and function-level imports, does not run the code, and would miss importlib or other dynamic imports. The 110-module closure counts module-level imports only. The TypeScript analysis covers apps/web app, components and lib with grep; package internals and test files were not graphed. I counted dependencies inside tests/ and scripts/ (sys.path inserts, private-name imports) but did not map them module by module. I did not check whether any LangGraph checkpoint stores classes by import path, so the module moves proposed here carry that open question. The project's PreToolUse hook refused one read-only grep because its pattern named the provider master key file; I reran it on the constant name DEFAULT_KEY_FILE. Per the ground rules, I did not rerun verification profiles or any runtime check, and the only file written is scratch output in .checks/reviews/review-2026-11-12-09-52-30/sweep-boundaries/py_edges.tsv.
